```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
                      fig.height = 4, dpi = 80)
library(hyperutils)
```

This vignette puts the pieces together into one script that reads a dataset,
checks it, runs the analysis, writes every table and figure to a folder, and
records what was done. It then shows how to verify the numbers against a
known answer and how the package behaves on a larger study.

## The shape of a reproducible script

A script that a colleague, a reviewer or you in a year can run again has five
parts: a header, the settings, the data, the analysis and the output. Put
every decision in the settings block, so that it is visible in one place.

```r
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# File:     pk_analysis.R
# Purpose:  Non-compartmental analysis and exploratory figures, study XYZ
# Author:   A. Analyst
# Version:  1.0
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
library(hyperutils)

# --- settings ---------------------------------------------------------
data_file <- "data/xyz001.csv"
out_dir   <- "output"
lloq      <- 0.5
units     <- list(time = "h", conc = "ng/mL", dose = "mg")
opt       <- hp_nca_options(lloq = lloq, blq_rule = "tmax-zero-missing",
                            auc_method = "linear-up-log-down",
                            dose_unit = "mg", conc_unit = "ng/mL")

# --- data -------------------------------------------------------------
d <- hp_read_data(data_file)

# --- analysis ---------------------------------------------------------
res <- hp_nca(d, options = opt, route = "oral", groups = "DOSEGRP")

# --- output -----------------------------------------------------------
hp_save_table(res$parameters, "nca_parameters.csv", out_dir)
```

The rest of this vignette fills in that outline and runs it on the example
data, writing to a temporary folder.

## The settings block

```{r settings}
out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "workflow")
lloq    <- 0.5
units   <- list(time = "h", conc = "ng/mL", dose = "mg")
opt     <- hp_nca_options(lloq = lloq,
                          blq_rule = "tmax-zero-missing",
                          auc_method = "linear-up-log-down",
                          dose_unit = "mg", time_unit = "h", conc_unit = "ng/mL")
d <- hp_read_data(hp_example_file())
```

## Step 1: check the data

Describe the dataset and look for problems before any analysis. The tables
below go into the data section of a report.

```{r qc}
e <- hp_eda_prepare(d, dvid = "DVID", lloq = lloq, color = "DOSEGRP")
data_summary <- hp_eda_data_summary(e)
missing_vals <- hp_eda_missing(e)
covariates   <- hp_eda_table(e, hp_eda_tspec(
  kind = "summary", scope = "subjects", vars = c("WT", "AGE"),
  by = "DOSEGRP", overall = TRUE))
data_summary[1:6, ]
```

Stop early when the data are not what you expect. A few lines of plain R make
the script fail loudly instead of producing a wrong analysis:

```{r checks}
stopifnot(
  "no dose records"        = any(d$AMT > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
  "duplicate subjects"     = !anyDuplicated(d[d$EVID == 1, "ID"]),
  "negative concentrations" = all(d$DV >= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
)
```

## Step 2: figures of the data

```{r figures}
profiles <- hp_eda_plot(e, hp_eda_spec(
  name = "profiles", title = "Concentration over time", kind = "line",
  x = "TAFD", y = "DV", color = "DOSEGRP", pk_only = TRUE, log_y = TRUE), units)
profiles[[1]]
```

## Step 3: the analysis

```{r nca}
res <- hp_nca(d, options = opt, route = "oral", groups = "DOSEGRP")
res
```

The options object records every setting of the analysis. Printing it, or
saving it, documents the analysis:

```{r options}
str(res$options[c("auc_method", "blq_rule", "lloq", "steady_state")])
str(res$options$lz[c("method", "min_points", "min_adj_r2")])
```

## Step 4: write everything

```{r write}
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
files <- c(
  hp_save_table(data_summary,    "data_summary.csv",   out_dir),
  hp_save_table(missing_vals,    "data_missing.csv",   out_dir),
  hp_save_table(covariates,      "covariates.csv",     out_dir),
  hp_save_table(res$parameters,  "nca_parameters.csv", out_dir),
  hp_save_table(res$summary,     "nca_summary.csv",    out_dir, digits = 4),
  hp_save_table(res$lambda_z,    "nca_lambda_z.csv",   out_dir),
  hp_save_table(res$profiles,    "nca_profiles.csv",   out_dir),
  hp_save_plots(profiles,        "profiles",           out_dir, 7, 5, dpi = 72)
)
figs <- hp_nca_plots(res, hp_nca_figure_options(units = units))
files <- c(files, unlist(lapply(names(figs), function(nm)
  hp_save_plot(figs[[nm]], paste0("nca_", nm), out_dir, 7, 5, dpi = 72))))
length(files)
head(basename(files), 8)
```

## Step 5: record the session

The last lines of a script should record what produced the files: the package
version, the date and the R session.

```{r record}
cat("hyperutils", as.character(hp_version()), "\n")
cat("R", R.version.string, "\n")
cat("Date", format(Sys.Date()), "\n")
```

```{r cleanup}
unlink(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)
```

Run the whole script from a shell with `Rscript pk_analysis.R`; a numbered
folder per run (for example `output/2026-01-31`) keeps the history.

## Verifying the numbers

Before trusting any NCA software on a regulatory analysis, check it on data
whose answer is known. For an intravenous bolus into a one-compartment model,
`C(t) = (D / V) exp(-k t)`, so without noise the area to infinity is exactly
`D / (V k)`, the clearance is `V k`, the half-life is `log(2) / k` and the
volume of distribution is `V`.

```{r verify}
D <- 100; V <- 40; k <- 0.15
tt <- c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24)
known <- rbind(
  data.frame(ID = 1, TIME = 0, AMT = D, DV = NA, EVID = 1, MDV = 1, CMT = 1),
  data.frame(ID = 1, TIME = tt, AMT = 0, DV = D / V * exp(-k * tt),
             EVID = 0, MDV = 0, CMT = 1))
chk <- hp_nca(known, route = "bolus")$parameters
data.frame(
  parameter = c("AUCINF_OBS", "CL_OBS", "VZ_OBS", "THALF"),
  estimated = unlist(chk[1, c("AUCINF_OBS", "CL_OBS", "VZ_OBS", "THALF")]),
  exact     = c(D / (V * k), V * k, V, log(2) / k),
  row.names = NULL)
```

The estimates agree with the exact values to rounding error. The default
linear-up/log-down rule is exact for a mono-exponential decline; the linear
rule is not:

```{r verify-linear}
lin <- hp_nca(known, options = hp_nca_options(auc_method = "linear"),
              route = "bolus")$parameters
c(exact = D / (V * k), log_down = chk$AUCLAST + chk$CLAST / chk$LAMZ,
  linear = lin$AUCLAST + lin$CLAST / lin$LAMZ)
```

The package's own test suite repeats checks of this kind for every method
and rule, and compares the C++ kernels with plain R implementations.

## Larger studies

The areas and the terminal-phase regressions run in compiled code, and the
bookkeeping around them is vectorised. To see the scaling, repeat the example
study with new subject numbers.

```{r scale}
bigger <- function(k) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(k), function(i) { x <- d; x$ID <- x$ID + 24 * (i - 1); x }))
}
big <- bigger(10)                      # 240 subjects
length(unique(big$ID))
rb <- hp_nca(big, route = "oral", lloq = lloq)
nrow(rb$parameters)
```

On a current laptop this analysis of several hundred profiles takes about a
second, and the time grows in proportion to the number of profiles. The
tables of a thousand-subject study still print and save in moments, which makes
it practical to re-run the whole analysis whenever the data change.

A few habits keep large analyses quick:

* Read the data once with `hp_read_data()` and pass the data frame around.
* Use `hp_nca_summary()` on the parameter table when you only want other
  statistics or strata; there is no need to repeat the analysis.
* Draw the individual-profile pages only when needed
  (`hp_nca_figure_options(individual = FALSE)`).
* Save figures at the resolution you need: `dpi = 72` for drafts and 300 for
  reports.
